hints: Think about what the unit $\text{m}^{-3}$ is telling you - it means number per unit volume, so start by working out the volume of this piece of wire from its length and cross-sectional area.
walkthrough:
**What Number Density Means**
Think of number density $n$ as how tightly packed the free electrons are - the number of free electrons in each cubic metre of metal. So you need total number divided by total volume.

**Find the Volume Then Divide**
The wire is a cylinder, so its volume is area times length:
$$V = A \times L = 1.5 \times 10^{-6} \times 1.8 = 2.7 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}^3$$
Then:
$$n = \frac{N}{V} = \frac{2.3 \times 10^{23}}{2.7 \times 10^{-6}} = 8.5 \times 10^{28} \text{ m}^{-3}$$

hints: You have two separate ideas to link together - charge passing a point in a time, and the slow drift of many electrons through the wire. Start by thinking how to get the current from $172 \text{ C}$ and $2.5$ minutes.

Now recall how current is related to number density $n$, area $A$, drift speed $v$ and electron charge $q$. Remember to convert the time to seconds and use $q = 1.60 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$ before rearranging for $v$.
Combine your two steps as $v = I/(nAq)$ with $I = 172/150$. Check your powers of ten carefully - $n$ is huge ($10^{28}$) so expect a very tiny speed.
walkthrough:
**Get the Current First**
Current is simply charge per second. The time must be in seconds, not minutes:
$$t = 2.5 \times 60 = 150 \text{ s}$$
$$I = \frac{Q}{t} = \frac{172}{150} = 1.15 \text{ A}$$

**Link Current to Drift Speed**
Inside the metal, this same current is carried by all the free electrons drifting slowly along. That link is:
$$I = nAvq$$
where $n = 8.5 \times 10^{28} \text{ m}^{-3}$ from part (a), $A = 1.5 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}^2$, and each electron carries charge $q = 1.60 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$. Rearrange for the drift speed $v$:
$$v = \frac{I}{nAq}$$

**Put the Numbers In**
$$v = \frac{1.1467}{(8.5 \times 10^{28}) \times (1.5 \times 10^{-6}) \times (1.60 \times 10^{-19})}$$
$$v = \frac{1.1467}{2.04 \times 10^{4}} = 5.6 \times 10^{-5} \text{ m s}^{-1}$$
This tiny value makes sense - electrons drift only fractions of a millimetre per second, even though the electrical signal travels almost instantly.
Final answer: $I = 1.15 \text{ A}$, $v = I/(nAq) = 5.6 \times 10^{-5} \text{ m s}^{-1}$
